tracks.title: Our cosmic address
tracks.summary: Start here: what space is, how we measure it, and where we are in it.

lessons.title: What is space?
lessons.summary: Where space begins, and what is (and isn't) out there.
keyIdeas: Space is usually said to begin about 100 kilometres above Earth, where the air becomes too thin for planes to fly.
It isn't completely empty: it holds thin gas, dust, light and radiation, but far less matter than any vacuum we can make on Earth.
With no air to carry it, sound can't travel through space.
Objects in sunlight heat up while those in shadow get extremely cold, so space isn't simply 'hot' or 'cold'.

lessons.title: Light-years: measuring huge distances
lessons.summary: Why astronomers measure distance in years.
keyIdeas: A light-year is a distance, not a time: how far light travels in one year.
That's about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth; light from the nearest other star, Proxima Centauri, takes about 4.2 years.
Looking at distant objects means looking back in time: we see them as they were when their light set off.

sources.title: Basics of Space Flight: The Solar System

lessons.title: Our address in the universe
lessons.summary: From planet to star to galaxy to the whole universe.
keyIdeas: Earth is one of eight planets orbiting the Sun.
The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy, the Milky Way.
The Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies.
Together, all matter, energy, space and time make up the universe, which is about 13.8 billion years old.

tracks.title: The Solar System
tracks.summary: The Sun, its planets and moons, and the small worlds in between.

lessons.title: Meet the Solar System
lessons.summary: Our Sun and everything that orbits it.
keyIdeas: The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the Solar System's mass.
Eight planets orbit the Sun: four small rocky ones close in, and four giants farther out.
Beyond the planets are dwarf planets like Pluto and countless icy bodies in the Kuiper Belt.

lessons.title: The Sun, our star
lessons.summary: The star at the centre of it all.
keyIdeas: The Sun is a star: a giant ball of hot gas, mostly hydrogen and helium.
In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, releasing the energy that lights and warms Earth.
About 109 Earths would fit side by side across its face.
It's roughly 4.6 billion years old, about halfway through its life.

lessons.title: The rocky planets
lessons.summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
keyIdeas: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner, rocky planets, with solid surfaces.
Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
Mars has the largest volcano in the Solar System, Olympus Mons.
Earth is the only planet known to have life, and liquid water on its surface.

lessons.title: The giant planets
lessons.summary: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
keyIdeas: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
Uranus and Neptune are ice giants, with more water, ammonia and methane.
None of them has a solid surface to land on.
All four have rings, though Saturn's are by far the brightest.

lessons.title: Moons
lessons.summary: Our Moon, and the many others in the Solar System.
keyIdeas: A moon is a natural object that orbits a planet, or another body such as a dwarf planet or asteroid.
Earth's Moon probably formed about 4.5 billion years ago from debris after a giant collision.
The same side of the Moon always faces Earth.
Jupiter and Saturn each have more than 90 known moons, and some, like Europa and Enceladus, hide oceans under their ice.

lessons.title: Dwarf planets, asteroids and comets
lessons.summary: The small worlds left over from the Solar System's birth.
keyIdeas: Dwarf planets, like Pluto and Ceres, are round but haven't cleared their path around the Sun of other objects.
Asteroids are rocky leftovers from the Solar System's formation; most orbit between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets are balls of ice and dust that grow glowing tails when they come near the Sun.
Studying these small worlds tells us what the early Solar System was made of.

tracks.title: Stars
tracks.summary: How stars are born, shine and die.

lessons.title: What is a star?
lessons.summary: Giant balls of gas that make their own light.
keyIdeas: A star is a huge ball of gas that shines because of nuclear fusion in its core.
Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
A star's colour shows its surface temperature: blue stars are the hottest, red ones the coolest.
Every star you can see with your eyes at night is in our own galaxy.

lessons.title: The life of a star
lessons.summary: From birth to red giant, white dwarf or something stranger.
keyIdeas: A star's mass decides how long it lives and how it ends.
Stars like the Sun shine for about 10 billion years, then swell into red giants and leave behind white dwarfs.
The most massive stars burn out in just a few million years.
Many elements in your body, like carbon and oxygen, were made inside stars.

lessons.title: Supernovae
lessons.summary: The explosions that end some stars, and seed new ones.
keyIdeas: A supernova is an exploding star, which can briefly outshine its whole galaxy.
It happens when a very massive star's core collapses, or when a white dwarf takes on too much matter.
Supernovae scatter heavy elements into space, which end up in new stars and planets.
What's left behind can be a neutron star or a black hole.

lessons.title: Black holes
lessons.summary: Where gravity wins completely.
keyIdeas: A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
Many form when massive stars collapse at the end of their lives.
Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of times the Sun's mass, sit at the centres of most large galaxies.
In 2019 astronomers released the first image of one, in the galaxy M87.

tracks.title: Galaxies and the universe
tracks.summary: Star cities, our Milky Way, and how it all began.

lessons.title: What is a galaxy?
lessons.summary: Vast collections of stars held together by gravity.
keyIdeas: A galaxy is a huge collection of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity.
Galaxies come in three main shapes: spiral, elliptical and irregular.
The nearest large galaxy, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
There are billions of galaxies in the observable universe.

lessons.title: The Milky Way
lessons.summary: Our home galaxy.
keyIdeas: The Milky Way is our home galaxy, a barred spiral about 100,000 light-years across.
The Solar System sits in one of its spiral arms, about 26,000 light-years from the centre.
At its heart is a supermassive black hole called Sagittarius A*.
From a dark place on Earth it appears as a faint band of light across the night sky.

lessons.title: The Big Bang
lessons.summary: How the universe began, and why it's still growing.
keyIdeas: The Big Bang theory says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding ever since.
It wasn't an explosion into space: space itself has been stretching.
Evidence includes the faint glow left over from the early universe, the cosmic microwave background.
The universe is still expanding today, and the expansion is speeding up.

lessons.title: Dark matter and dark energy
lessons.summary: Most of the universe is something we can't see.
keyIdeas: Most matter in the universe is invisible 'dark matter' that doesn't give off, reflect or block light.
We know it's there from its gravity: galaxies spin too fast to hold together without it.
Dark energy is something else: a mysterious effect that is speeding up the universe's expansion.
Ordinary matter, everything we can see, makes up only about 5% of the universe.

tracks.title: Other solar systems
tracks.summary: Planets around other stars, and where life might be possible.

lessons.title: What is an exoplanet?
lessons.summary: Planets that orbit other stars.
keyIdeas: An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.
The first one around a Sun-like star was found in 1995; today more than 6,000 are confirmed.
Most are found by spotting tiny dips in a star's light as a planet passes in front of it.
Many are unlike anything in our own Solar System.

lessons.title: Kinds of planets out there
lessons.summary: Hot Jupiters, super-Earths and more.
keyIdeas: Astronomers sort exoplanets into gas giants, Neptune-like planets, super-Earths and rocky planets.
Super-Earths are bigger than Earth but smaller than Neptune, a size our Solar System doesn't have.
Some 'hot Jupiters' orbit so close to their stars that a year lasts only a few days.
A star with its planets is called a planetary system; ours is one of many.

lessons.title: The habitable zone
lessons.summary: Where liquid water, and maybe life, could exist.
keyIdeas: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface.
Too close and water boils away; too far and it freezes.
Being in the zone doesn't mean a planet has life, or even water.
Earth sits comfortably inside the Sun's habitable zone.

tracks.title: How we explore
tracks.summary: Rockets, orbits, telescopes, space stations and rovers.

lessons.title: How rockets work
lessons.summary: Pushing gas one way to go the other.
keyIdeas: A rocket pushes hot gas out of its engine in one direction, which pushes the rocket the other way.
Rockets carry their own oxygen supply, so their engines work in space where there's no air.
To stay in orbit around Earth, a spacecraft must travel about 28,000 km/h sideways.
Most rockets are built in stages that drop away once their fuel is used up.

lessons.title: Orbits
lessons.summary: Falling around a planet without ever hitting it.
keyIdeas: An orbit is the curved path one object follows around another because of gravity.
A spacecraft in orbit is always falling towards Earth, but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.
Low Earth orbit (LEO) reaches up to about 2,000 km; the space station flies at around 400 km.
Geostationary satellites, about 36,000 km up, circle once a day and seem to hang still over one spot.

sources.title: Basics of Space Flight: Planetary orbits

lessons.title: Space telescopes
lessons.summary: Why we put telescopes above the atmosphere.
keyIdeas: Telescopes in space see more clearly because Earth's air blurs and blocks some kinds of light.
Hubble, launched in 1990, has made more than 1.5 million observations.
The James Webb Space Telescope sees infrared light, letting it look through dust and back towards the first galaxies.
Different telescopes study different kinds of light, from radio waves to X-rays.

lessons.title: The International Space Station
lessons.summary: A home and laboratory in orbit.
keyIdeas: The International Space Station is a laboratory orbiting about 400 km above Earth.
People have lived on board continuously since November 2000.
It circles Earth about every 90 minutes, roughly 16 times a day.
Crews study how living in space affects the human body, among thousands of other experiments.

lessons.title: Rovers
lessons.summary: Robot explorers on other worlds.
keyIdeas: A rover is a robotic vehicle that drives across another world's surface.
NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers are exploring Mars, looking for signs of ancient life.
Commands take several minutes to reach Mars, so rovers drive partly on their own.
Rovers have explored the Moon too, starting with the Soviet Lunokhod 1 in 1970.
